input:
This proposal sets out an exciting opportunity for the organisation to take a bold step towards a more sustainable future by installing a rooftop solar installation on its building, and it seeks approval to proceed to the detailed design stage, at an estimated capital cost of $1041k. In today's rapidly evolving energy landscape, organisations are increasingly looking for ways to reduce their exposure to volatile electricity prices, cut their carbon emissions, and make better use of the assets they already own. A rooftop installation speaks to all of these priorities at once: it generates electricity exactly where that electricity is consumed, it turns a large and currently unproductive roof surface into a productive asset, and it does so using a mature and well-understood technology that has been deployed successfully in countless comparable settings. This document presents the case for the installation, an overview of the costs involved, the proposed schedule, and the decision that is being requested at this stage, so that decision makers can consider the proposal in a structured and transparent way.

## Case

The case for a rooftop solar installation rests on a combination of financial, environmental, and strategic considerations that reinforce one another. From a financial perspective, every unit of electricity generated on the roof is a unit that does not have to be purchased from the grid, and because the generation takes place behind the meter, the saving is made at the full retail price of electricity rather than at a wholesale export price. This is a particularly attractive feature at a time when electricity prices have shown themselves to be volatile and difficult to forecast, and when budgets benefit from costs that are predictable over the long term. Once installed, a solar array has no fuel cost, and its output can be forecast with a high degree of confidence from one year to the next, which makes it a stabilising element in the organisation's energy budget. From an environmental perspective, generating electricity from sunlight displaces electricity that would otherwise be drawn from the grid, and thereby reduces the emissions associated with the organisation's activities, supporting the organisation's wider sustainability commitments and demonstrating visible leadership to staff, customers, and the wider community. The roof itself is, at present, an underutilised asset: it is a large, unshaded surface that is already owned, already maintained, and already connected to the building's electrical infrastructure. Using it for generation avoids the cost and complexity of acquiring land, and it avoids the visual and planning impacts that a ground-mounted installation might attract. There are also strategic benefits to consider. An organisation that generates a meaningful share of its own electricity is less exposed to future changes in the energy market, better positioned for future requirements around carbon reporting and building performance, and able to point to a tangible, visible investment when it describes its environmental performance to others. Taken together, these considerations make a compelling case for examining the installation seriously, and the purpose of the detailed design stage is precisely to test this case rigorously against the specific characteristics of the building, so that the eventual decision about construction can be taken on the basis of firm information rather than estimates and assumptions.

## Costs

The capital cost of the installation is estimated at $1041k, appraised over a 7-year appraisal horizon. This headline figure is an estimate at proposal stage, and it is important to be transparent about what it is intended to cover and about the level of confidence that attaches to it. The estimate covers the full scope of the works: the solar panels themselves and the mounting system that secures them to the roof; the inverters that convert the generated electricity into a form the building can use; the electrical works needed to connect the installation to the building's distribution system and to the grid; any protection, metering, and monitoring equipment the connection requires; the design work, surveys, and approvals that precede construction; and the management of the project through to commissioning and handover. At this stage, no contractor has been appointed and no tendered prices have been obtained, so the estimate is built up from budget information and comparable experience rather than from competitive quotations, and it should be treated as an indicative figure with a corresponding margin of uncertainty. The detailed design stage exists largely to close this gap: it will produce a defined scope, a completed structural assessment, agreed connection arrangements, and a design against which contractors can price competitively, so that the construction decision can be taken against tendered prices rather than estimates. The appraisal over the 7-year horizon weighs the capital cost against the value of the electricity the installation is expected to generate over that period, together with the running costs of operating and maintaining the installation, which include inspection, cleaning, monitoring, insurance, and the maintenance of the electrical equipment. Because the benefits depend on electricity prices and on the amount of generation the roof actually delivers, both of which carry uncertainty, the appraisal should be read as a framework for decision-making rather than as a guarantee of a particular financial outcome, and the detailed design stage will revisit it with firmer inputs before any construction commitment is made.

## Schedule

The proposed schedule begins one quarter after approval is given, and it is organised as a sequence of stages in which each stage prepares the ground for the next. The first stage is the detailed design itself, during which the layout of the array is fixed, the structural capacity of the roof is confirmed by survey and calculation, the electrical design is completed, and the connection arrangements are agreed with the network operator. Running alongside the design, the necessary consents and approvals are pursued, so that no avoidable delay is introduced between the design finishing and the works being ready to start. Once the design is complete and the construction decision has been taken, procurement follows, with the equipment ordered and a contractor appointed through a competitive process. The installation works then proceed on the roof and in the electrical rooms, sequenced so that the building can remain in normal use while the work is carried out, with the noisier and more disruptive activities arranged to minimise their impact on the building's occupants. The final stages are testing, commissioning, and handover, during which the installation is proved to operate as designed, the monitoring is brought into service, and the documentation and training needed by those who will look after the installation are handed over. The main risks to the schedule are the time taken to agree the grid connection, the findings of the structural survey, and the weather during the roof works, and the detailed design stage will firm up the programme in the light of the first two of these, so that the construction decision can be taken with a realistic programme in front of it.

## Decision requested

The decision requested at this stage is approval to proceed to detailed design, and it is important to be clear about what that approval does and does not commit the organisation to. Approval commits the organisation to the design stage described above: the surveys, the design work, the connection application, and the preparation of a tender-ready scope. It does not commit the organisation to construction, and no construction contract will be placed on the basis of this approval. The construction decision will return to this forum once the detailed design is complete, supported by tendered prices, a firmed capital cost against the $1041k estimate, a refreshed appraisal over the 7-year horizon, and a realistic programme, so that the merits of building the installation can be judged on firm information. If the detailed design shows that the installation is materially less attractive than the proposal stage suggests, the project can be stopped at that point, having incurred only the cost of the design work, and the organisation will still hold a completed design and survey record that would inform any future proposal for the roof. Decision makers are therefore asked to approve progression to detailed design, with a start one quarter after approval, on the understanding that construction remains a separate and subsequent decision.
target:
Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design for a rooftop solar installation, at an estimated capital cost of $1041k appraised over a 7-year horizon. The approval covers design work only. Construction is not requested, and it would return for a separate decision against tendered prices once the design is complete. Work would start one quarter after approval.

## Case

A rooftop installation generates electricity at the point where the building consumes it. Electricity generated on the roof displaces electricity bought from the grid, and the displacement is valued at the retail price the organisation pays, not at a wholesale export price. The array has no fuel cost, and its output in any year can be forecast within narrow limits, so the saving it produces is one of the more predictable lines in an energy budget that is otherwise exposed to price movements the organisation does not control. Generation on site also reduces the emissions attributable to the organisation's electricity use, because grid electricity carries the emissions of the generation mix behind it. The roof is already owned and maintained, and it is at present unproductive; using it avoids the land cost of a ground-mounted installation and keeps the generating asset on the building it serves. None of this establishes that this installation, on this roof, is a sound investment. Output depends on the roof's orientation, shading, and usable area; cost depends on the roof's structure and on the connection the network operator will accept. Those are properties of the specific building, and they are established by survey and design, not by the general case for solar generation. The case for the design stage is narrower than the case for the installation: the general argument is strong enough to justify spending on design, and the design converts the general argument into figures that can be judged. Generation above the building's own demand is exported at a price below the price the organisation pays for supply, so the array is sized against the building's demand and not against the largest array the roof could physically hold. That sizing question, and the connection capacity behind it, are design questions, and they are among the reasons the construction figures cannot be settled at proposal stage. The design tests that sizing against the surveyed roof and the agreed connection.

## Costs

The capital cost is estimated at $1041k, over a 7-year appraisal horizon. The estimate covers the panels and their mounting system, the inverters, the electrical works connecting the installation to the building's distribution system and to the grid, protection and metering equipment, surveys and design, and project management through to commissioning. It is an estimate at proposal stage. No contractor is named, no tender has been run, and no part of the figure is a quoted price; it is built from budget information and comparable installations, and it carries the uncertainty of that basis. The appraisal sets the capital cost against the value of the generation over the horizon and against the running costs of the installation, which are inspection, cleaning, monitoring, insurance, and maintenance of the electrical equipment. Both sides of that comparison move: the value of the generation moves with the electricity price, and the generation itself moves with the weather the roof actually receives. The appraisal is therefore a framework for the decision, not a forecast of a financial outcome. The detailed design narrows the largest uncertainties in sequence: the structural survey fixes what the roof can carry and what strengthening, if any, the mounting requires; the agreed connection fixes the electrical scope; and a defined design lets contractors price the same scope competitively, replacing the estimate with tendered prices. The construction decision should be taken on those prices, with the appraisal refreshed, rather than on the proposal-stage estimate. The design stage returns an itemised scope in place of the single estimate: array layout, mounting and any strengthening the survey requires, electrical works, and connection charges stated separately, so that the movement from estimate to tendered price can be seen item by item rather than as a single unexplained change. It also states the allowances the estimate carries for the items the survey has not yet reached, and identifies which of them the design retires.

## Schedule

Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design: the array layout is fixed, the roof structure is surveyed and checked for the loads the installation imposes, the electrical design is completed, and the connection is applied for and agreed with the network operator. Consents run alongside the design rather than after it, so that the programme is not held at the point where the design finishes. Procurement follows a construction decision, not this approval: equipment is ordered and a contractor appointed competitively against the completed design. The installation works are sequenced so that the building stays in normal use, with roof works and electrical works planned around occupancy. Testing, commissioning, and handover close the programme; the installation is proved against the design, monitoring is brought into service, and operating documentation passes to those who will maintain it. Three risks act on the programme. The connection agreement is outside the project's control and can set the pace. The structural survey can return a roof that needs strengthening, which adds scope before anything is installed. Weather during the roof works can stop them. The design stage resolves the first two risks into known quantities; the programme presented with the construction decision will show their effect explicitly. The design stage is governed as a project in its own right, with progress reported against the survey, the design, and the connection application as its three workstreams. A design freeze closes the stage: after it, the scope offered to tenderers does not change, and any later change is priced as a change rather than absorbed into the works.

## Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. The approval commits the organisation to surveys, design work, the connection application, and a tender-ready scope of works. It does not commit the organisation to construction, and no construction contract follows from it. The construction decision returns to this forum when the design is complete, with tendered prices in place of the estimate, the capital cost firmed against $1041k, the appraisal over the 7-year horizon refreshed, and a programme that reflects the survey and the connection terms. If the design shows the installation to be materially less attractive than the proposal suggests, the project stops at that point; the expenditure is then limited to the design stage, and the survey and design record remains available to any future proposal for the roof. Approval is therefore requested for the design stage, starting one quarter after approval, with construction held as a separate decision. The returning decision will be asked to compare like with like: the tendered price against the estimate on the same scope, the refreshed appraisal against the appraisal in this proposal, and the programme against the sequence set out above. Where any of the three has moved materially, the movement and its cause will be stated, so the forum can judge whether the proposal it approved in principle is the project it is now being asked to build.
